<meta>continues from previous page: ...The previous discussion concerned the proper forms of ritual and the consequences of their decline.</meta>

...cannot be misrepresented; this is also the path of teaching and instruction. A question was asked regarding the section from the Eight-Row Dance to the sacrifice at Mount Tai <note>referring to Analects 3.1 through 3.6, which discuss the usurpation of royal rituals by noble families</note>. Because these rituals were extinguished, the sense of grief and pain is entirely consistent with the intent of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* <note>a historical chronicle attributed to Confucius that evaluates events with moral judgment</note>. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> said, "This is correct."

○ The Master said: "A gentleman <term>Junzi</term> <gloss>an exemplary person</gloss> has no reason to compete. If he must, then it is surely in archery! Bowing and yielding, they ascend the hall. Descending, they drink together. Such is the competition of a gentleman." <note>The original note indicates the character for competition is pronounced in the departing tone to specify its meaning.</note>

"Bowing and yielding while ascending" refers to the Great Archery Ritual. One advances with three bows and then ascends the hall. <note>Master Hu</note>

In the ritual of archery, the Director of Archery <term>Sisha</term> <gloss>the official overseeing the match</gloss> organizes three pairs of archers. These three pairs emerge from their waiting area, face west, and bow. When they arrive at the north of the steps, they bow. At the steps themselves, they bow again. This is what is meant by "three bows and then ascending the hall."

This refers to the completion of the archery. They bow and descend to wait for all the other pairs of archers to finish. Then the winners bow to the losers, and the losers ascend to take <margin>Explanation of sounds</margin> up the cup and drink while standing. <note>Master Hu says: When the shooting is finished, they bow facing north just as they did when ascending. After the archery is over, they return to their original positions.</note>

The other pairs finish their shooting in the same way. This is what is meant by "bowing and descending after the shooting."

<summary>Confucius explains that a gentleman avoids petty competition, participating only in ritual archery where respect and etiquette are maintained. The commentary provides a technical breakdown of the bowing and drinking ceremonies required during these formal matches.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Archery, Ritual, Junzi, Etiquette, Sisha, Great Archery, Zhou Dynasty, competition</keywords>
